newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary, Romania to discuss joint military force.
newsitem.headline: Hungary, Romania to discuss joint military force.

text.p: Hungary expects to sign a military agreement with Romania on Monday which analysts believe will enhance both countries' credentials as potential NATO members.

The agreement on the protection and exchange of military secrets was expected to be signed at a meeting of the two east European states' defence ministers, who may also approve the setting up of a joint military unit, Hungarian ministry sources say.

The meeting comes as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright visits Europe on a tour which is to include Russia, where she plans to unveil new details of NATO's proposals for European security and the alliance's plans to expand eastwards to embrace former communist states.

Analysts believe the proposed Hungarian-Romanian accords could mean Romania joining current favourites Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary in the first group of states to be invited to join NATO at the alliance's next summit in Madrid in July.

Hungary's defence minister Gyorgy Keleti told Reuters he hoped an agreement on the exchange of military data, Hungary's first with an East European neighbour, would be signed during the meeting, to be held in the eastern Hungarian city of Debrecen, near the Romanian border.
"It will entitle the two countries to exchange important military information," he said. "So far Hungary only has such agreements with the United States, Germany and Sweden."

Romania's Foreign Minister Adrian Severin said last month Keleti's Romanian counterpart Victor Babiuc would be bringing a proposal to set up a Romanian-Hungarian military force modelled on 1950s Franco-German unit which was seen as a symbol of post-war reconciliation.

Laszlo Valki, head of international law at Budapest's Lorand Eotvos University, told Reuters if the two proposals are accepted it will have an important psychological effect on the two countries and on their efforts to join NATO.

"Symbolically this is very significant as it gives a psychological message to both peoples that the two countries really are friends," he said. "And the joint unit will show NATO that the closest cooperation is possible in peacekeeping and joint exercises."

Bucharest's new centrist government, elected last November after seven years of rule by ex-communists, is seeking to boost Romania's chances of early admission to NATO by developing a new partnership with Hungary.

New president Emil Constantinescu appointed two leaders of Hungary's ethnic minority to his government while Severin's first trip abroad was to Hungary to exchange ratified basic treaty documents with his Hungarian counterpart, Laszlo Kovacs.

The treaty, signed in September, aims to end old quarrels by guaranteeing Romania's western borders and ensuring the rights of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians and is seen as vital to the ambitions of Romania and Hungary to move closer to Europe and NATO.

Hungary's state secretary at the Defence Ministry responsible for NATO integration, Istvan Gyarmati, said Hungary had floated the idea of the joint force with Romania's previous government but had received a cool response.
"The previous government was quite hesitant to give a definite answer," Gyarmati told Reuters. "Now we've got it from the Romanians."

Relations between Budapest and Bucharest were soured last April when Babiuc's predecessor Gheorghe Tinca said a decision to allow Hungary into NATO before Romania could prompt an arms race in the region.
However, Romania's new government has taken a softer line towards its neighbours that has won it friends among some NATO members who say it has enhanced its chances of early membership.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said last month Romania's improved relations with Hungary and Ukraine had boosted its chances of quick admission. French President Jacques Chirac told Constantinescu 10 days ago Paris strongly backed Bucharest's drive to be among the first East European nations to join the alliance.
